## Part 4: Tools and Resources
Reference: https://aisharedresponsibility.com/tools/

Interactive tools for applying the SRF to real deployments.

### Regulation Discovery Wizard
URL: https://aisharedresponsibility.com/tools/regulation-discovery/

4-step wizard identifying applicable regulations by jurisdiction, risk tier, deployment context, and industry vertical. Outputs a layer-mapped regulatory profile with PDF export. References L1-L5 accountability assignments.

### Controls Assessment (AICM)
URL: https://aisharedresponsibility.com/tools/controls-assessment/

Assess control implementation status against the SRF across all five layers (L1 AI Business & Usage through L5 AI Model Provider).

### Layer Matrix
URL: https://aisharedresponsibility.com/tools/layer-matrix/

Visual matrix of accountability assignments across all five SRF layers and four operating models (AI-SaaS, AI-PaaS, Agent-PaaS, IaaS).

### Policy Pyramid
URL: https://aisharedresponsibility.com/tools/policy-pyramid/

Governance policy hierarchy showing how L1 (AI Business & Usage) policy cascades down through L2-L5.

### Security Controls
URL: https://aisharedresponsibility.com/tools/security-controls/

Security-specific control reference with SRF layer and persona mapping.

### SRF Stress Test
URL: https://aisharedresponsibility.com/tools/srf-stress/

Accepts a plain-language AI deployment scenario and stress-tests it against SRF accountability rules. Identifies unassigned accountability gaps.

### Vendor Risk Assessment
URL: https://aisharedresponsibility.com/tools/vendor-risk/

Maps the AI vendor landscape to the SRF for vendor risk, third-party risk, and procurement teams. Sorts AI suppliers into seven categories: (1) core AI platform and infrastructure (L4/L5, IaaS and AI-PaaS), (2) pre-trained model and algorithm providers (L5, AI-PaaS), (3) AI-enabled SaaS applications (L3, AI-SaaS), (4) agentic AI and autonomous systems (L3/L4, Agent-PaaS), (5) data, labeling and retrieval services (L2), (6) AI consulting and professional services (cross-layer), and (7) software, VARs and distributors (L3/L4). Each category states which responsibilities the vendor owns versus which stay with the customer, the attestation baseline (SOC 2, ISO 27001, ISO 42001, ISO 9001, FedRAMP), and the specific evidence to request. Adds a three-tier risk model, a cross-cutting AI-risk checklist (prompt injection direct and indirect, model and weight supply chain, agent authorization and override, retrieval/RAG integrity, liability for AI-generated harm), and an attestation reference explaining what each certification does and does not prove. Categories 3 and 4 close gaps in a typical third-party questionnaire. Machine-readable as /data/vendor-risk.json.

### Vendor Risk Assessment How-To
URL: https://aisharedresponsibility.com/tools/vendor-risk/how-to/

Five-step workflow for running a vendor risk assessment with the SRF: tier the vendor on data sensitivity, autonomy, and SRF depth; place it on the SRF layers; split accountability with one owner per responsibility; demand evidence rather than assertions; and write the responsibility boundary into the contract. Includes a downloadable XLSX VRA workpaper with an Instructions tab, a Risk Tiers tab, an Accountability Split tab, an Attestation Reference tab, an Attestation Mapping tab, a Contract Clauses tab, an RFP Questions tab, and a Question Bank of 37 evidence asks across all seven categories with response, evidence, and decision columns.

### Incident Response Playbooks
URL: https://aisharedresponsibility.com/tools/ir-playbooks/

Day-2 incident response playbooks for when an AI accountability boundary fails. Covers a common first-fifteen-minutes triage and seven scenario playbooks: (1) prompt injection leading to data exfiltration (L3), (2) model or training-data poisoning (L5/L2), (3) autonomous agent took a harmful or unauthorized action (L3/L4), (4) sensitive data leaked through prompts, logs, or output (L2/L4), (5) harmful, infringing, or non-compliant output (L1/L3), (6) sub-processor or model supply-chain breach (L5/L4), and (7) silent model change broke a control (L5). Each playbook resolves who leads the response per operating model (AI-SaaS, AI-PaaS, Agent-PaaS, IaaS) from the SRF responsibility matrix, then lists triage steps, what to demand from the vendor, and what evidence to preserve. The vendor asks align with the contract clauses on the vendor risk page. Machine-readable as /export/playbooks.json.

### Red Team Scoping Tool
URL: https://aisharedresponsibility.com/tools/redteam-scope/

Scopes an AI red team engagement with the SRF accountability overlay. Pick an operating model (AI-SaaS, AI-PaaS, Agent-PaaS, IaaS), autonomy tier, and optional industry vertical; the tool resolves each layer to one of three tiers: testable directly (the target org owns the layer), authorization required (the layer is shared or provider-evaluated; record what was granted before testing), or out of scope (the provider owns the layer outright). Pre-assigns one named finding owner per layer, flags layers with no authorization reference on file, surfaces related threats from the crosswalk per layer, and lists standard evidence-handling obligations. Produces a signable scoping record exportable to PDF and JSON, reusing the Accountability Decision Record's sign-off pattern. Supplies only the accountability overlay; methodology is the OWASP GenAI Red Teaming Guide, attack taxonomy is NIST AI 100-2.

Machine-readable matrix exports for GRC ingestion: /export/matrix.csv (flat CSV of the accountability matrix) and /export/srf-oscal-catalog.json (OSCAL 1.1.2 catalog; groups are SRF layers, controls are layer-by-operating-model accountability cells).

### System Instructions
URL: https://aisharedresponsibility.com/tools/prompts/

Copy-ready prompts for grounding AI assistants in the SRF. Core instruction enforcing one accountable party per activity. Role variants: executive, auditor, developer, legal/procurement. Sector context parameters for all six verticals.

### AI Security Lifecycle
URL: https://aisharedresponsibility.com/framework/security-lifecycle/

How the SRF supplies the accountability axis across the AI security lifecycle. Security work at every stage needs three answers that no threat catalog, control matrix, or severity score supplies: who must authorize the activity, who owns each result, and who signs the residual risk. One accountable party per activity; "shared" is not a valid final answer. The framework stays in its accountability lane: it does not define attack techniques, threats, or test methodology (BIML, OWASP AI Exchange, OWASP GenAI, MITRE ATLAS, NIST AI 100-2 own that), does not define control content or benchmarks (CIS, CSA AICM, OWASP AI Exchange controls own that), does not score severity (AIVSS owns that), and creates no new regulation.

Six categories, each with the SRF contribution and the open gap:

1. Threat modeling and risk analysis. Contribution: bounds the analysis to the layers you own under your operating model and names the persona who owns each risk. Serves BIML, OWASP AI Exchange, NIST. Site has the threat-to-accountability crosswalk (/data/threats.json), the layer model, the compare page, and the glossary. Gap: extending the crosswalk beyond the sixteen AI Exchange matrix threats to the full BIML and ATLAS sets.

2. Adversarial testing and red teaming. Contribution: engagement scoping and rules of engagement. The operating model determines which layers the customer may test at all; personas pre-assign finding ownership before the first probe. This is the proven category: LLMs referencing the site already use its structure to scope AI red team engagements unprompted. Serves OWASP GenAI Security Project, SANS, NIST. Site has the Red Team Scoping Tool (/tools/redteam-scope/), which reads the crosswalk and returns testable, authorization-required, and out-of-scope layers per operating model, plus the SRF Stress Test and the Accountability Decision Record sign-off pattern. No open gap; methodology comes from the OWASP GenAI Red Teaming Guide and NIST AI 100-2, the tool supplies only the accountability overlay.

3. Secure development and AI supply chain. Contribution: names who attests at each handoff in the model and data supply chain and who verifies it, per operating model. Serves CoSAI, CIS, OWASP AI Exchange. Site has the Vendor Risk Assessment and the supply-chain threats in the crosswalk. Gap: an attestation handoff map as data.

4. Control implementation and benchmarking. Contribution: control ownership. Every catalog says what good looks like; none say who at your company owns each control under your deployment model. The vertical schemas prove the pattern with 258 controls carrying an accountable persona. Serves CIS, CSA, OWASP AI Exchange, NIST. Site has the AICM and Security Controls assessments, six vertical schemas, the OSCAL catalog, and a CIS Controls card on the compare page. Thirty-four controls across the six vertical schemas carry a control-level `cis` mapping key (CIS Controls v8.1), verified against the official 18-control list and the April 2026 AI/LLM Companion Guide. No open gap at the control level mapped; safeguard-level (N.N) mapping remains future work.

5. Vulnerability management and finding remediation. Contribution: routing. Severity scoring says how bad; the SRF says whose queue a finding goes in and who signs acceptance if it will not be fixed. Serves OWASP GenAI Security Project (AIVSS) and coordinated disclosure practice. Site has the finding routing reference (/data/finding-routing.json), which resolves an AIVSS- or CVSS-scored finding to an accountable persona and breach action by SRF layer and operating model, and the Incident Response Playbooks (machine-readable at /export/playbooks.json). No open gap; AIVSS's own numeric severity-band cut points remain TBD pending its full v0.8 documentation, so routing keys on the qualitative band.

6. Detection, monitoring, and incident response. Contribution: who leads when a boundary fails, what to demand from the counterparty, and which evidence obligations survive. Serves SANS, CIS, CoSAI. Site has the Incident Response Playbooks and the thresholds SLI/SLO schema with an OCSF evidence plane. The playbooks now cite the Red Team Scoping Tool and the finding routing reference as upstream inputs (see /export/playbooks.json `upstream_inputs`). Workforce readiness is already served by the NICE mapping.

MOSAIC context: MOSAIC (Multi-Organization Secure AI Coordination) launched April 28, 2026 with eight founding initiatives (BIML, CIS, CSA, CoSAI, NIST, OWASP AI Exchange, OWASP GenAI Security Project, SANS). Its shared taxonomy, built on OpenCRE by the OWASP AI Exchange, links terms, controls, and concepts across the standards but carries no accountability. Binding SRF canonical IDs (from /ids.json) into OpenCRE makes the SRF the accountability axis of that taxonomy: any threat or control node can then resolve to an accountable persona under a stated operating model. The binding itself is published at /export/opencre-srf.json (OpenCRE-conformant Standard documents for the framework, five layers, eight personas, four operating models, and all twenty accountability matrix relations, with three proposed CRE anchors verified against the live OpenCRE graph: 225-553 Organizational AI security controls, 663-200 Technical AI security controls, 803-457 Protection against AI-Specfic Threats) and /export/opencre-srf.csv (the same set in the MyOpenCRE import format). Generated deterministically by build/generate_opencre_binding.py; sections without a proposed anchor await a working session with the OpenCRE maintainers.

### Threat-to-Accountability Crosswalk
URL: https://aisharedresponsibility.com/data/threats.json

Machine-readable crosswalk mapping each named AI security threat to the SRF layer where it lands and the accountable persona per operating model. Threat definitions and IDs belong to their external sources; the file adds the three accountability answers no threat catalog carries. Covers the sixteen threats in the OWASP AI Exchange AI security matrix, keyed by the AI Exchange permalink slug, with mappings to the OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025), MITRE ATLAS technique IDs, and BIML LLM24 risk IDs, plus related control IDs from the vertical schemas. Each threat carries an accountability object for AI-SaaS, AI-PaaS, Agent-PaaS, and IaaS, naming one accountable persona and party per model and recording the counterparty obligation where the matrix says shared. Threats: direct prompt injection (L3), indirect prompt injection (L3), evasion (L5), runtime model poisoning (L4), development-environment model poisoning (L5), data poisoning of train or fine-tune data (L2), supply-chain model poisoning (L5), disclosure in output (L5), model inversion and membership inference (L5), development-time data leak (L2), model exfiltration (L5), runtime model leak (L4), development-time model leak (L5), AI resource exhaustion (L4), input data leak (L3), and output contains conventional injection (L3).

### Finding Routing Reference
URL: https://aisharedresponsibility.com/data/finding-routing.json

Machine-readable routing reference closing the loop opened by the threat crosswalk and the red team scoping tool: a finding scored by AIVSS (OWASP AI Vulnerability Scoring System, v0.8, extends CVSS v4.0 with agentic risk-amplification factors) or CVSS routes by SRF layer and operating model to one accountable persona and one breach action. Twenty entries, one per layer (L1-L5) by operating model (AI-SaaS, AI-PaaS, Agent-PaaS, IaaS), each carrying an accountable persona, accountable party, and a kebab-case breach_action escalation ladder across four severity bands (critical, high, medium, low) consistent with the /thresholds/gap-register.json breach_action convention. Referenced from the security lifecycle page and cited by the Incident Response Playbooks as an upstream input. AIVSS's own published severity-band numeric cut points are TBD pending its full v0.8 scoring calculator documentation; routing keys on the qualitative band, not a specific score cutoff. The SRF does not score severity; AIVSS and CVSS own that.

### Changelog
URL: https://aisharedresponsibility.com/changelog/

Dated record of site changes grouped by release. Tracks CoSAI SRF v1.0 (released May 28, 2026) and v2.0 work in progress. Core framework reference follows official CoSAI and OASIS releases; industry vertical schemas are independently proposed extensions flagged experimental.
